Measles is a serious infectious disease. "Infectious" means it is caused by a tiny germ — specifically a virus — that gets inside your body and makes you sick. The disease attacks your respiratory system (your nose, throat, and lungs) and also causes a very distinctive red rash all over your skin.

Measles is one of the most contagious diseases ever known to humans. "Contagious" means it spreads from person to person very easily. In fact, if one person with measles is in a room, nearly 9 out of 10 unprotected people in that same room will get infected. That is an extraordinary rate of spread — very few other diseases come close to this.

Measles is caused by a specific virus called the Morbillivirus. A virus is a microscopic particle — far too small to see with the naked eye — that invades the cells of your body and multiplies inside them, causing illness. Importantly, measles is not caused by bacteria, so antibiotics (medicines that fight bacteria) do not treat it.

The measles virus travels through the air. When an infected person coughs, sneezes, or even just breathes or talks, they release tiny invisible droplets containing the virus. These droplets float in the air for up to two hours even after the infected person has left the room. If you breathe those droplets in, or touch a surface they landed on and then touch your eyes, nose, or mouth, you can get infected.

This airborne spread is exactly why measles spreads so fast and so widely.

Anyone who has never had measles and has never been vaccinated against it can get the disease. Historically, it has been most common in young children, but it can infect people of any age. Once you recover from measles, your body builds strong immunity, meaning you cannot get it again. Similarly, if you receive the measles vaccine, you become protected.

Measles develops in clear stages. After you are infected, there is a silent period (called the incubation period) of roughly 10 to 14 days during which you feel perfectly fine but the virus is multiplying inside you.

After that, the disease appears in two main stages:

Stage 1 — The Early Stage (lasts 2–4 days):
This stage looks very much like a bad cold or flu. You will have:

  • High fever (often above 38.5°C / 101°F, sometimes reaching 40°C / 104°F)
  • A persistent cough
  • A runny nose
  • Red, watery eyes (a condition called conjunctivitis, where your eyes look irritated and sore)
  • Feeling generally exhausted and unwell

A very important and unique sign during this early stage is the appearance of Koplik's spots — tiny white or bluish-white dots that appear inside the mouth (on the inner cheeks), looking like grains of salt surrounded by red. These spots are unique to measles and help doctors identify the disease before the rash even appears. They disappear after a couple of days.

Stage 2 — The Rash Stage (begins around day 3–5):
The most recognizable sign of measles is the rash — flat, red or reddish-brown spots that often merge into each other to form larger blotchy patches. The rash typically:

  • Starts on the face (often near the hairline and behind the ears)
  • Spreads downward over the next few days, covering the neck, trunk, arms, legs, and feet
  • Lasts about 5 to 6 days before fading

When the rash appears, the fever often reaches its highest point, and the person feels their sickest.

Many people think of measles as a simple childhood illness, but this is a serious misunderstanding. Measles can be life-threatening, especially for:

  • Young children (under age 5, especially under age 1)
  • Malnourished children (those who are not getting enough nutrition)
  • People with weakened immune systems
  • Pregnant women

The serious complications that measles can cause include:

  • Pneumonia — a dangerous lung infection that is the most common cause of measles-related death in children
  • Encephalitis — swelling of the brain, which can cause permanent brain damage, intellectual disability, or death (occurs in roughly 1 in 1,000 cases)
  • Blindness — measles can damage the cornea (the outer layer of the eye), especially in children who are deficient in Vitamin A
  • Severe diarrhea and dehydration, which can be fatal in very young or malnourished children
  • Ear infections, which can lead to permanent hearing loss
  • Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE) — a rare but always fatal brain disease that can develop years after a measles infection, causing progressive brain deterioration

Before vaccines were developed, measles killed millions of children around the world every year.

Prevention is primarily done through vaccination. The measles vaccine is extraordinarily effective — it is usually given as part of the MMR vaccine, which protects against Measles, Mumps, and Rubella (three diseases in one shot). Two doses of this vaccine provide about 97% protection against getting measles. This vaccine is one of the greatest achievements of modern medicine.

Treatment is focused on managing symptoms, because — as with most viruses — there is no specific medicine that kills the measles virus itself. A doctor may recommend:

  • Rest and fluids to prevent dehydration
  • Medication to reduce fever (like paracetamol or ibuprofen)
  • Vitamin A supplements, which significantly reduce the risk of severe complications and death, particularly in children
  • Treatment for any secondary infections (like bacterial pneumonia) that might develop alongside measles

Measles was so widespread for centuries that it was considered almost inevitable that every child would get it. In the 20th century alone, before the vaccine was introduced in the 1960s, measles killed an estimated 200 million people worldwide.

Thanks to widespread vaccination, measles was officially eliminated from many countries (meaning it was no longer spreading continuously within those countries). For example, the United States declared measles eliminated in the year 2000. However, "eliminated" does not mean "gone forever" — when vaccination rates drop (because of hesitancy or access issues), the virus can travel from other countries and cause outbreaks again. This is exactly what has happened in various countries in recent years.

Globally, measles still causes the deaths of tens of thousands of children every year, primarily in regions where vaccines are not widely available.

Grammatically, measles is interesting. Even though it ends in -s, it is treated as a singular noun. You say:

  • "Measles is a serious disease." ✅ (not "measles are")
  • "She has measles." ✅
  • "The child caught measles." ✅
  • "Measles was once a leading killer of children." ✅

This pattern is shared with similar disease names like mumps, rabies, and diabetes — all of which end in -s but are grammatically singular.

You would never say "a measle" (there is no singular form used in standard English). The word always appears as measles, whether you are talking about one case or many.
Measles is a highly contagious, potentially life-threatening viral disease that causes fever, cough, red eyes, and a characteristic full-body red rash, and is best prevented through vaccination.
